title: Static Initialization Order Fiasco bugs reported by Coverity Scan
body:
### Tested versions

Reproducible in 4.5 dev 3.
Probably reproducible since 4.0, and also likely in 3.x.


### System information

All

### Issue description

The "[Static Initialization Order Fiasco](https://www.google.com/search?q=static+initialization+order+fiasco)" (SIOF) is a well known "gotcha" in c++:

> The static initialization order problem is a very subtle and commonly misunderstood aspect of C++. Unfortunately it’s very hard to detect — the errors often occur before main() begins.

> In short, suppose you have two static objects x and y which exist in separate source files, say x.cpp and y.cpp. Suppose further that the initialization for the y object (typically the y object’s constructor) calls some method on the x object.

> That’s it. It’s that simple.

> The tough part is that you have a 50%-50% chance of corrupting the program. If the compilation unit for x.cpp happens to get initialized first, all is well. But if the compilation unit for y.cpp get initialized first, then y’s initialization will get run before x’s initialization, and you’re toast. E.g., y’s constructor could call a method on the x object, yet the x object hasn’t yet been constructed.

I'm creating this issue to centralize tracking of handling of this issue as we have some discussions in RocketChat but no "goto" place for newbies to SIOF.

Note that I'm not an expert in SIOF, only have dealt with its problems before, and attempt to write _to the best of my knowledge_. Sometimes there may be language guarantees that can be used to get around the problem.

Note that SIOF also occurs on destruction, and this is especially potentially relevant for singletons, which are an attempt to deal with the problem but may not be able to guarantee order of destruction where singletons are in different translation units (grok seems to indicate this is a problem).

Another traditional way to solve this problem is to use explicit create and destroy (or initialize and terminate) functions for globals, and explicitly order construction / destruction from a single "app" global, and forego built-in constructors / destructors completely for these globals.

At the moment we have issues particularly for certain types which cannot currently safely have static lifetime, yet this rule is broken in quite a few areas, these are the worst offenders:

* Variants
* Strings / StringNames
* Singletons
* Containers (especially `HashMap`)

Consider that containers often have destructors which call `ERR` macros to report failures. This is UB, because the `ERR` machinery (and `Variant` used in printing) may be destroyed _before_ the container.

Variants depend on Variant pools and Strings, Strings depend on Variants, the list of interdependencies is long. Also the memory allocator machinery e.g. `Memory::mem_usage` is often depended on.

### Likely results
* Undefined behaviour (likely varying with platforms / compilation settings)
* Crash on exit / pause on exit as OS attempts to recover

### Steps to reproduce

Run Coverity Scan.

### Minimal reproduction project (MRP)

Run Coverity Scan.

### Examples

class_db.cpp:
```
HashMap<StringName, HashMap<StringName, Variant>> ClassDB::default_values;
```
> CID 464582: (#1 of 1): Initialization or destruction ordering is unspecified (GLOBAL_INIT_ORDER)
destructor_uses_global_object: The destructor of global object ClassDB::default_values_cached itself makes use of global object StringName::Table::allocator defined in another compilation unit. The order of destruction is unspecified, so the destructor of ClassDB::default_values_cached might be called after StringName::Table::allocator has already been destroyed.

webrtc_peer_connection.cpp:
```
StringName WebRTCPeerConnection::default_extension;
```
> CID 464578: (#1 of 1): Initialization or destruction ordering is unspecified (GLOBAL_INIT_ORDER)
destructor_uses_global_object: The destructor of global object WebRTCPeerConnection::default_extension itself makes use of global object StringName::Table::allocator defined in another compilation unit. The order of destruction is unspecified, so the destructor of WebRTCPeerConnection::default_extension might be called after StringName::Table::allocator has already been destroyed.

## Discussion
The problem is rather pervasive, we've started having discussions at ways of attacking the problem, and will be brought up in a core meeting to ensure more maintainers are familiar with it.

In a large number of cases with `Strings` and `HashMap` / `HashSet`, what seems to be happening is that one contributor has made a PR storing strings in a global in a cpp, and then many other contributors have copied this technique assuming that it was safe.

One way of addressing these "convenience globals" might be to have something like a "global store" per module, with explicit create / destroy functions called by the app. This would require some significant re-engineering, and care to prevent dependency creep.

The use of singletons (e.g. `Engine`, `OS`, `Servers` etc) might have to be re-evaluated, particularly with their lack of order guarantees over multiple translation units. Simple globals can offer better SIOF guarantees, with explicit create / destroy functions (I personally tend to use this approach in preference to singletons).

#### Static asserts
It would be nice to make this foolproof and statically assert that certain classes were not used with static lifetime, but there doesn't appear to be an easy way of doing this in c++.

We spent some time with Grok attempting to come up with a solution, and it may be possible to have a runtime check `DEV_ASSERT` or similar that fails quickly when classes are misused in terms of lifetime, perhaps having a global bool set to true in `main()` and `DEV_ASSERT` that this is true in the constructors of the "not allowed" classes.

<details>

```
#include <stdexcept>

class NoStatic {
private:
    static bool is_initialized;
    void checkStatic() {
        if (!is_initialized) {
            throw std::runtime_error("NoStatic cannot be used with static lifetime");
        }
    }

public:
    NoStatic() {
        checkStatic();
    }
};

bool NoStatic::is_initialized = false;

int main() {
    NoStatic::is_initialized = true; // Set flag at start of main
    NoStatic obj; // OK: Created in main
    return 0;
}
```

</details>

#### What *can* be safely used as globals?
Trivial types with trivial destructors (e.g. basic types `uint32_t` etc) and also `Vector3`, `Plane` etc. Types with non-trivial destructors are often not safe to use. `LocalVector` may be okay, with the aforementioned trivial types.

Containers with "machinery" (COW etc) may not be safe to use.

Of course containers that are used as globals should not be accessed within the global app construction / teardown, and are only safe to use outside these times.
